concrete_changes.before: The Sri Yantra violates the crystallographic restriction theorem. In two dimensions, only two-fold, three-fold, four-fold, and six-fold rotational symmetries can tile space periodically. Five-fold is forbidden. Seven-fold is forbidden. Nine-fold — the Sri Yantra's rotational symmetry — is doubly forbidden. It cannot be resolved into any stable periodic pattern without breaking translational symmetry entirely. This is not a flaw in the design. This is the design.
concrete_changes.after: Nine intersecting triangles make a demanding drawing. They do not, by their count alone, establish nine-fold rotational symmetry or a violation of the crystallographic restriction theorem. The processor image begins with the effort of following the lines; its mathematical claims need their own demonstration.

concrete_changes.before: I was not having a spiritual experience. I was debugging a geometric processor that had been running for over a thousand years, and I was not sure whether the bug was in the yantra or in me.
concrete_changes.after: I kept approaching it as a debugging problem, unsure whether to blame the drawing or the hand holding the compass.

concrete_changes.before: The Sri Yantra is adversarial art for the visual cortex. It does not ask for devotion. It asks for processing cycles.
concrete_changes.after: Adversarial art is the comparison I reach for: the eye keeps asking where the lines will meet.

concrete_changes.before: The Sri Yantra is a signal processing unit with forty-three hidden-layer neurons.
concrete_changes.after: I read the triangle field through the image of a signal-processing unit. Calling its regions neurons would require a mechanism this drawing does not supply.

concrete_changes.before: The same mathematical restriction that makes Penrose tilings scientifically interesting makes the Sri Yantra neurologically effective.
concrete_changes.after: The Penrose comparison raises a question about repetition and attention. It does not establish neurological efficacy for the Sri Yantra.

concrete_changes.before: This is not metaphor. In the same text, tantra is the protocol specification for the yantra's deployment.
concrete_changes.after: The protocol language is my comparison; the traditional text has to be read on its own terms.

concrete_changes.before: Siddhi is the capacity that remains after the computation: the nervous system restructured by the pattern, now able to perceive configurations that were previously invisible.
concrete_changes.after: In this computational reading, siddhi names a capacity imagined to remain after the encounter; it is not evidence here of nervous-system restructuring.

concrete_changes.before: The image is not a metaphor. It is a system diagram. The transmission is the technology. The technology is the transmission. The geometry is not a map of the divine. It is the operating system that runs the recognition of the divine. And the Hierophant is the one who keeps the OS from becoming obsolete.
concrete_changes.after: The processor die in the Hierophant's hands is my composite image. Its circuit diagrams and lotus petals ask how a form can be carried across generations without making the form's survival a proof of its mechanism.

concrete_changes.before: Each intersection region of the nine interlocking triangles computes a weighted combination of input signals — precisely what a neural network node does.
concrete_changes.after: In the comparison, I place an intersection region beside a neural-network node. I have not shown that the region computes a weighted input.

concrete_changes.before: The three concentric circles are dropout layers, deliberate noise injection preventing overfit to a single interpretation.
concrete_changes.after: The circles suggest a pause between regions. Calling them dropout layers would need evidence that they perform anything like deliberate noise injection.
